topic.name: Sums of Infinite Geometric Series Given in Sigma Notation

question.explanation:
Notice that the given series is a geometric series because it is in the form $\displaystyle \sum ar^n.$

The sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of a geometric series is given by the formula

\[ S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad |r| < 1, \]

where $a_1$ is the first term and $r$ is the common ratio.

The first term is \[ a_1 = 10\left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^1 =5. \]

The common ratio is \[ r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{10\left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^2}{10\left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^1} = \dfrac{1}{2}. \]

So, the sum of the series is \[\begin{align*} \sum_{n=1}^\infty 10\left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^{n} &= \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)}\\[5pt] & = 5 \cdot \dfrac{2}{1}\\[5pt] & = 10. \end{align*}\]

example.title: Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Expressed in Sigma Notation

question.explanation:
First, note that the index $n$ starts from $3.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\displaystyle \sum ar^n.$

In this case, the first term is $a_3,$ and so the sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of this geometric series is given by

\[ S_\infty = \dfrac{a_3}{1-r}, \qquad |r| < 1. \]

For the first few terms, we have:

\begin{align*} a_3 &= \dfrac{4}{9}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{3} = \dfrac{4}{9}\left(\dfrac{27}{64}\right) = \dfrac{3}{16}\\[5pt] a_4 &= \dfrac{4}{9}\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{4} =\dfrac{4}{9}\left(\dfrac{81}{256}\right) = \dfrac{9}{64} \end{align*}

The common ratio is \[ r = \dfrac{a_4}{a_3} = \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{9}{64}\right)}{\left( \dfrac{3}{16}\right)} = \dfrac{9}{64} \cdot \dfrac{16}{3} = \dfrac{3}{4} . \]

So, the sum of the series is

\[\begin{align*} \sum_{n=3}^\infty \dfrac{4}{9}\left(\dfrac 3 4\right)^{n} &= \dfrac{a_3}{1-r}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{3}{16}\right)}{\left(1 - \dfrac{3}{4}\right)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{3}{16}\right)}{\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{16} \cdot 4 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4} . \end{align*}\]

example.title: Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Expressed in Sigma Notation With an Arbitrary Starting Index

question.explanation:
First, note that the index $n$ starts from $3.$ However, it is still a geometric series because it is in the form $\displaystyle \sum ar^n.$

In this case, the first term is $a_3,$ and so the sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of this geometric series is given by

\[ S_\infty = \dfrac{a_3}{1-r}, \qquad |r| < 1. \]

For the first few terms, we have:

\begin{align*} a_3 &=\dfrac{25}{27}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^{3} = \dfrac{25}{27} \left(\dfrac{27}{125}\right) = \dfrac{1}{5}\\[5pt] a_4 &=\dfrac{25}{27}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^{4} = \dfrac{25}{27} \left(\dfrac{81}{625}\right) = \dfrac{3}{25} \end{align*}

The common ratio is \[ r = \dfrac{a_4}{a_3} = \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{3}{25} \right)}{\left( \dfrac{1}{5} \right)} = \dfrac{3}{5} . \]

So, the sum of the series is

\begin{align*} \sum_{n=3}^\infty\dfrac{25}{27}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)^{n} &= \dfrac{a_3}{1-r}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{1}{5} \right)}{\left(1 - \dfrac{3}{5}\right)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left( \dfrac{1}{5} \right)}{\left(\dfrac{2}{5}\right)}\\[5pt] &= \left( \dfrac{1}{5} \right) \cdot \dfrac{5}{2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} . \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Expressed in Sigma Notation With an Arbitrary Starting Index

question.text: Evaluate the geometric series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac 5{2}\left(-0.4\right)^{2n}.$ Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
The sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of a geometric series is given by

\[ S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad |r| < 1. \]

The first term is

\[ a_1 = \dfrac 5{2}\left(-0.4\right)^{2(1)}= \dfrac 5{2}\left(-0.4\right)^2 \]

and the second term is

\[ a_2 =\dfrac 5{2}\left(-0.4\right)^{2(2)} = \dfrac 5{2}\left(-0.4\right)^4. \]

Therefore, the common ratio is

\[ r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{\dfrac 5{2}\left(-0.4\right)^4}{\dfrac{5}{2}\left(-0.4\right)^2} = \left(-0.4\right)^2=0.16 . \]

So, the sum of the series is

\begin{align*} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac 5{2}\left(-0.4\right)^{2n}&= \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\dfrac 5{2}\left(-0.4\right)^2}{1-0.16}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\dfrac 5{2}(0.16)}{0.84}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{0.4}{0.84}\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{10}{21}} . \end{align*}

example.title: Evaluating an Infinite Geometric Series Expressed in Non-Standard Form Using Sigma Notation

question.text: Evaluate the geometric series $\displaystyle\sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac 9{4}\left(-\dfrac 13\right)^{2n}.$ Do not round the answer.
question.explanation:
The sum to infinity $S_\infty$ of a geometric series is given by

\[ S_\infty = \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}, \qquad |r| < 1. \]

The first term is

\[ a_1 = \dfrac 9{4}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{2(1)}= \dfrac 9{4}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2 \]

and the second term is

\[ a_2 =\dfrac 9{4}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{2(2)} = \dfrac 9{4}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^4. \]

Therefore, the common ratio is

\[ r = \dfrac{a_2}{a_1} = \dfrac{\dfrac 9{4}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^4}{\dfrac{9}{4}\left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2} = \left(-\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^2=\dfrac 1{9} . \]

So, the sum of the series is

\begin{align*} \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac 9{4}\left(-\dfrac 13\right)^{2n}&= \dfrac{a_1}{1-r}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\dfrac 9{4}\left(\dfrac{1}{9}\right)}{\left(1-\dfrac 1{9}\right)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\left(\dfrac 1{4}\right)}{\left(\dfrac 8{9}\right)}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac 1{4}\cdot\dfrac{9}{8}\\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{9}{32}} . \end{align*}
